_about.what: The Study Guide's PROSE SCAFFOLDING for one cert, keyed by topic slug. A topic IS a guide section, 1:1, so the key is the section anchor. The facts themselves are not here - each one lives on the question that tests it, in that question's `guide` block.
_about.why: A guide fact and its question shared scope, topic, source, sourceSection, dates and media, so holding them apart meant six duplicated fields per fact and two build checks to keep them honest. Housing the fact on the question makes that consistency structural instead of enforced.
_about.positioning: A cheat sheet, not a manual. It states what a rider needs in order to pass and points at the agency document for everything behind it. Never comprehensive, never explanatory, and it may never read as a substitute for the state manual or a course.
_about.consequence: The guide can never carry something the bank does not test. A fact worth reading is a fact worth asking, so anything the guide should say has to be authored as a question with a `guide` block.
_about.shape: A topic holds an `opener` and an ordered list of `groups`. A group holds an `id`, a `heading`, a `leadIn` and optional `media`. Group order is array order, and `groups` may be empty while a topic is being authored.
_about.membership: A question joins a group through `guide.group` and sorts inside it by `guide.order`. A null group is legal and renders above the topic's first heading, so questions can be authored before the grouping is settled. There is no manifest of question ids here, deliberately: it would duplicate what the question already declares, and two owners for one fact stop agreeing.
_about.ordering: `guide.order` is sparse - 10, 20, 30 - so a fact can be inserted between two others without renumbering the rest.
_about.kinds: `guide.kind` decides how a fact renders: `rule` is a bare assertion on one line, `value` is a label and a value rendered into a dl, `steps` is an ordered procedure rendered into an ol. Mixing kinds is what stops a section reading as a wall of declarative sentences.
_about.text: `guide.text` is the fact as the guide states it. Null falls back to the question's explanation, which under §5 rule 6b is the same assertion - so a question only carries its own `text` where the guide wants it shorter or shaped for a dl.
_about.originalText: `opener` orients a reader arriving at the topic; `leadIn` says what a group of facts is about. One or two sentences each and no more - connective text between individual facts is what makes a cheat sheet feel padded.
_about.scoping: A section resolves by resolving its questions, so scope needs no separate expression here. A group whose questions all resolve away renders nothing, which means a leadIn has to survive its group being only partly filled.
_about.media: A figure attaches to a GROUP and earns its place when the group is spatial or sequential - geometry, position, formation, or a sequence of actions. Never for a value or a rule. Signs are the exception: the sign IS the fact, so that image rides the question's own media.
_about.catchAll: The catch-all topic has no entry here. It carries weight 0 in every state, so it reaches no guide; it earns an opener the day a state weights it above zero.
_about.status: BAREBONES. Every topic carries an opener so the guide renders from the first question authored into it. Only signs-and-markings and space-management carry groups; every other topic collects its facts ungrouped until a grouping pass places them.

fit-to-ride.opener: Two questions before the engine starts: whether the law lets you ride, and whether your body and mind are in shape to.

gear-and-bike-check.opener: Everything settled before the bike moves: what protects you in a fall, and what tells you the machine is safe to take out.

basic-control.opener: The controls a motorcycle asks for that a car never does, and the habits that make reaching for them automatic.

visibility-and-communication.opener: Most collisions between a car and a motorcycle start with a driver who never saw one. Being seen is something a rider does on purpose.

space-management.opener: Where to sit in the lane, how much room to leave, and what changes when traffic closes in.

groups.heading: How much space to keep
groups.leadIn: Following distance is counted in seconds rather than car lengths: pick a fixed marker ahead, and count from the moment the vehicle in front passes it until you do.

groups.heading: Where to ride in the lane
groups.leadIn: A lane is wider than a motorcycle needs, and the whole of it is yours to use.

search-and-strategy.opener: Looking far enough ahead that you still have a choice left by the time you need one.

hazards-and-surfaces.opener: What the road puts under your tires and into your path, and what to do when the bike itself lets you down.

passengers-and-cargo.opener: A passenger or a load changes how the bike steers, leans and stops. Both are set up before you pull away, not after.

signs-and-markings.opener: Signs tell you what is coming and what is required, and most can be read from shape and color alone, before you are close enough to read the words.

groups.heading: What the shape tells you
groups.leadIn: The national standard reserves most shapes for one sign or one kind of sign, so those mean the same in every state. Rectangles are shared, and which way one stands is only a general guide.

groups.heading: What the color tells you
groups.leadIn: Color does the same job as shape, and the two agree: a sign that looks wrong for its message usually is not the sign you think it is.

groups.heading: Signs that state a rule
groups.leadIn: Regulatory signs give notice of a traffic law or regulation, so what one says is binding.

groups.heading: Speed signs
groups.leadIn: Some speed signs set a limit, and others give notice of one or recommend a speed. The words on the sign say which.

groups.heading: Traffic signals
groups.leadIn: What a signal asks of you depends on its color and on whether it is steady, flashing or dark.

groups.heading: Pavement markings and lanes
groups.leadIn: Lines and lanes painted on the road carry rules of their own, from crosswalks to turn lanes and bicycle lanes.

groups.heading: Roundabouts
groups.leadIn: Roundabouts keep traffic moving one way around a center island, with a set way to enter, ride and leave.

rules-of-the-road.opener: Some states test their traffic laws as part of the knowledge exam. Here are the rules a rider most needs, starting with who goes first.

groups.heading: Right-of-way
groups.leadIn: The law settles who goes first in each situation, and expects you to give way whenever insisting would cause a crash.

groups.heading: Officers, emergency vehicles and work zones
groups.leadIn: Officers, flaggers, and emergency and work vehicles all come before the usual order of traffic.

groups.heading: Turns
groups.leadIn: Where a turn starts and finishes, and when a red light still lets you make one.

groups.heading: School buses
groups.leadIn: A school bus's lights say when to slow, when to stop and how long to stay stopped.

groups.heading: Stopping and parking
groups.leadIn: Some places are closed to you even for a moment; others allow only a quick passenger stop.

groups.heading: Speed and lane use
groups.leadIn: Default speed limits, and the rules for the passing lane, slow traffic and changing lanes.

groups.heading: Phones, headphones and conduct
groups.leadIn: What the law bars while you ride: holding a phone, headphones that cut out traffic, and driving to intimidate.

groups.heading: Passing
groups.leadIn: Where a pass is allowed, how it has to end, and what you owe a vehicle you pass or that passes you.

groups.heading: Expressways
groups.leadIn: Joining an expressway, the lanes on it, and when you may stop on its shoulder.

groups.heading: Pedestrians and bicycles
groups.leadIn: Where crosswalks are, when you must stop for someone in one, and what a cyclist may do on the road.

groups.heading: After a crash
groups.leadIn: What the law asks of you at the scene, whoever was at fault.
